column1: What hardware component performs virtual-to-physical address translation on every memory access, and what happens when the translation is invalid?
column2: The Memory Management Unit (MMU) walks the page table in hardware to translate addresses; an invalid or missing mapping raises a page fault exception, trapping into the kernel.

column1: Why does static partitioning of physical RAM among processes fail as a memory isolation strategy?
column2: Programs don't know their load address at compile time, libraries can't be shared without duplication, memory footprints change dynamically, and buggy processes could still index outside fixed bounds—virtual memory solves all of these via per-process address spaces.

column1: What race condition occurs when two threads increment a shared counter without synchronization, and why?
column2: A 'lost update': both threads read the same initial value, increment independently, and write back identical results, permanently losing one increment because the read-modify-write is not atomic.

column1: Define the happens-before relation and give two ways it is established.
column2: Happens-before is a partial order guaranteeing that effects of operation A are visible to operation B. It is established via: (1) releasing a mutex happens-before a subsequent acquire of the same mutex, and (2) an atomic store-release happens-before an atomic load-acquire reading that value (also thread creation happens-before the spawned thread's first instruction).

column1: What do acquire and release memory ordering semantics guarantee, respectively?
column2: Release semantics ensure all prior writes become visible before the atomic store itself; acquire semantics ensure all subsequent reads observe memory state at least as recent as the atomic load.

column1: What is the 'everything is a file' principle in Unix, and what structure implements it?
column2: It means read()/write() system calls operate uniformly across disks, sockets, pipes, and devices. The file descriptor—an integer index into a per-process table—points to a kernel file description tracking offset, mode flags, and the underlying file object.

column1: What atomicity guarantee does Linux provide for pipe/socket writes under PIPE_BUF (4096 bytes), and why does it matter?
column2: Writes smaller than PIPE_BUF are atomic—concurrent writers cannot interleave data within a single message—which is a correctness requirement, not an optimization, enabling safe composition of shell pipelines and multi-writer IPC.

column1: What are CPU protection rings, and how do Ring 0 and Ring 3 differ on x86-64?
column2: Protection rings are hardware-enforced privilege levels. Ring 0 (kernel mode) allows unrestricted access to privileged instructions, control registers, and physical memory; Ring 3 (user mode) confines processes to a sandbox requiring explicit kernel interfaces (system calls) for privileged operations.

column1: What three mechanisms provide the only entry points into kernel code from a privilege-boundary perspective?
column2: (1) System calls—explicit userland requests via the syscall interface; (2) hardware interrupts/exceptions—asynchronous events like timers, disk I/O, or page faults vectored via the Interrupt Descriptor Table; (3) the scheduler, which multiplexes CPU cores independently of userland observation.

column1: What is the end-to-end principle in network architecture, and how does it shape the TCP/IP layering?
column2: Intelligence and reliability belong at the endpoints, while the network core stays simple and stateless. Routers forward IP packets statelessly based on destination prefixes alone; reliability, ordering, and congestion control are delegated entirely to transport-layer protocols (e.g., TCP) on end hosts.

column1: According to the CAP theorem, what must a distributed system sacrifice during a network partition?
column2: It must choose between Consistency (all nodes see the same data at the same time) and Availability (every request receives a response)—both cannot be fully guaranteed simultaneously when a partition occurs.

column1: Why is there no single universal 'now' in a distributed system?
column2: Because network message propagation has irreducible latency (bounded by the speed of light/electrical signal propagation), every node continues executing independently during that interval with no causal knowledge of concurrent remote operations, making a single global snapshot of state ambiguous.
